title: API Design, SOLID and Design Patterns
objectives: Design function and class APIs that are hard to misuse: explicit types, validated inputs, clear error paths, stable surfaces
State the five SOLID principles and give a concrete finance-system example of each
Recognise and apply Strategy, Observer, Adapter, Factory and Facade in trading-system contexts
Refactor branching logic into polymorphism where it buys extension without modification - and know when NOT to
motivation: The fee calculator worked perfectly for two years - then the desk added a bps fee model, and the change touched a 300-line if/else chain in the middle of order handling, with a missed branch found by the reconciler a week later. The cost was not the math; it was an API and structure that made extension dangerous. This lesson is about designing the seams of a system - APIs that cannot be misused, principles that guide where code should change, and the handful of patterns that recur in every trading codebase.

blocks.text: APIs: contracts that are hard to misuse

blocks.md: An API is a promise, and its quality shows under change and misuse. Design rules that pay for themselves: **make invalid states unrepresentable** - a `Side` enum beats a string that might say 'buy', 'BUY' or 'B'; **state units and types in the signature** (`int quantity`, `double price`) instead of in a comment; **make the happy path obvious and the error path explicit** - return a result or throw a specific exception, never a magic `-1`; **keep the surface small** - every public function is a promise you must keep through refactors; and **name for the domain** - `apply_fill` says more than `process`. Versioning belongs to the same discipline: a public API added to is easy, changed is expensive, so get the first version minimal and right.

blocks.caption: Same functionality, different contract: the second version cannot be called with a meaningless string, and errors are loud.

blocks.text: SOLID, grounded in a trading system

items: **S - Single Responsibility**: one reason to change per class. PnL *math* lives in a calculator, not inside the class that also loads positions from the database - a change in storage must never risk the arithmetic.

**O - Open/Closed**: open for extension, closed for modification. A new fee model should arrive as a *new class*, not as an edit inside the order-handling switch - which is exactly the incident in the motivation.

**L - Liskov Substitution**: any subclass must honour the base contract. A `SimulatedFeed : MarketDataFeed` that silently returns stale prices breaks every consumer that trusts the interface's promise of 'latest'.

**I - Interface Segregation**: many small interfaces beat one fat one. A listener that only wants trade prints should implement `TradeListener`, not implement eight empty methods of an `AllMarketDataListener`.

**D - Dependency Inversion**: depend on abstractions. The order router depends on a `MarketDataFeed` *interface*; a vendor SDK becomes an implementation detail swapped behind an Adapter - and replaced by a fake in tests.

blocks.md: **Strategy** in C++ is a small interface plus a `std::unique_ptr` to the implementation, held by a context class that knows nothing about concrete fees. The cost is one virtual call per event - irrelevant at desk scale, measurable only in the innermost latency loops, where patterns give way to branches measured with benchmarks. blocks.md: Patterns are vocabulary, not goals. Their value is that a name — "strategy", "observer", "adapter" — compresses a design decision into one word your team already understands, and their danger is that pattern-driven design produces architecture astronautics: four abstract classes to print a number. The professional filter is always the same: **what variation does this pattern buy me, and do I actually need that variation?**

blocks.title: The Strategy pattern, in a pricing-engine context
items: The variation you need: multiple pricing models (binomial tree, Black-Scholes, Monte Carlo) selected at runtime by instrument type.
Wrong turn: a `price()` function with a `switch (model)` over enum values, duplicated at every call site — every new model edits every switch.

Strategy: an abstract interface `Pricer { double price(const Option&) const; }`, one concrete class per model, and the *caller depends only on the interface*. Adding a model becomes adding a file, not editing a web of switches.

The cost you accepted: one virtual call per pricing (a pointer chase the CPU cannot inline) and one more layer to read. For a hot loop pricing a million options, that cost is real — and the fix is *not* to abandon the pattern but to hoist the dispatch out of the inner loop, or to use CRTP/templates for static polymorphism where the model is known at compile time.
The general lesson: patterns trade runtime indirection (or compile-time complexity) for changeability. The trade is good exactly when the variation is real, and waste when it is speculative.

blocks.title: SOLID, honestly stated
blocks.md: Single responsibility, open-closed, Liskov, interface segregation, dependency inversion — five heuristics that all reduce to: *depend on abstractions, keep responsibilities separable, and do not promise more than you honour*. They are heuristics, not laws; a 30-line script obeying all five is worse than a 30-line script that ignores them. The time to reach for them is when change hurts — that pain, not a checklist, is the signal.

blocks.title: Patterns are vocabulary, not goals
blocks.md: A two-branch if/else is clearer than a Strategy hierarchy; a Singleton 'for convenience' creates global state that makes tests order-dependent and parallelism fragile - prefer injecting instances. Reach for a pattern when you have the *recurring variation* it solves, not to decorate code. The failure mode is a framework of one-use abstractions nobody dares simplify.

Observer is everywhere in market data: the feed publishes updates, listeners subscribe. The design decision that matters is **lifetime ownership** - a listener that unsubscribes in its destructor, or the feed holding `weak` references, prevents the classic dangling-callback crash where the feed notifies a listener that was already destroyed. When you review an Observer design, ask exactly one question first: who owns the subscribers, and what happens when one dies mid-callback?

independentExercise.prompt: Design the public API for a `PositionBook` that applies fills and returns the updated position. Requirements: fills carry side/quantity/price; quantities are always positive on a fill; the book may go short; a zero or negative fill quantity is invalid; the class must be unit-testable without a database. Give the types and method signature, justify each API choice against 'hard to misuse' and SOLID, and sketch how a test would substitute dependencies if any existed.
hints: enum class Side, a Fill struct with validated-positive int quantity, a Position struct with signed quantity.
Decide the error path explicitly: throw a specific exception or return a result type - not a bool nobody checks.
SRP: the book tracks positions only; PnL math lives elsewhere. DIP: if persistence is needed later, it enters behind an interface.

commonMistakes: Strings or booleans as mode parameters ('buy' vs 'BUY') where an enum would make mistakes unrepresentable.
Silent error paths: returning -1 or false from an API whose callers never check it.
Forcing a pattern everywhere - a 2-line if/else does not need a class hierarchy.
Using a Singleton for convenience, then wondering why tests interfere with each other (global mutable state).
Publishing a fat interface 'for flexibility' that every implementer must stub out in eight empty methods.
Adding public API surface early ('we might need it') and paying to maintain it forever.
realWorldApplication: Exchange and vendor SDKs are consumed through Adapters; internal services publish Facades over their subsystems; and the stable, versioned APIs this lesson teaches are what let teams change internals while dozens of downstream consumers compile untouched.
quantFinanceApplication: Fee models, execution algorithms and risk checks are Strategies by construction on real desks, because they change weekly; the Apply-fill PositionBook API here mirrors production position keepers, where a signed-quantity contract and explicit invalid-fill errors are audited requirements.
summary: Good APIs make invalid states unrepresentable: domain types (enum class Side), units in the signature, explicit error paths, minimal surface.
SOLID in practice: one reason to change per class (SRP), extend by adding classes not editing switches (OCP), honour base contracts (LSP), small interfaces (ISP), depend on abstractions (DIP).
Strategy = interface + interchangeable implementations held by a context; it removes string/branch dispatch and buys extension without modification.
Observer (market data), Adapter (vendor SDKs), Factory (typed construction) and Facade (subsystem front doors) cover most trading-system needs.
Patterns are vocabulary for recurring problems, not decoration: measure the cost, avoid Singletons' global state, and prefer the simplest design that survives the actual rate of change.

quiz.prompt: Which statements are correct statements of SOLID principles?
options: Single Responsibility: a class should have one reason to change
Open/Closed: extend behaviour by adding code, not by editing existing switch statements
Dependency Inversion: high-level policy depends on abstractions, not concrete implementations
Liskov Substitution: subclasses may silently weaken the base class's guarantees
quiz.explanation: LSP says the opposite of the last option: every subtype must be usable wherever the base is expected, honouring its contract - a simulated feed that returns stale prices violates it.

quiz.prompt: A desk must support several interchangeable fee models selected at startup. Which pattern fits BEST?
quiz.explanation: Strategy encapsulates interchangeable algorithms behind one interface - fee models are the textbook case. Adapter translates foreign interfaces; Facade hides subsystem complexity; Singleton adds global state without solving variation.

quiz.prompt: Your team must integrate a third-party market-data SDK but wants its own Feed interface everywhere else. Which pattern is the standard answer?
quiz.explanation: An Adapter wraps the vendor SDK and exposes your Feed interface - the vendor stays an implementation detail that can be swapped or faked in tests.

quiz.prompt: Why does a Singleton make testing harder?
quiz.modelAnswer: A Singleton is global mutable state shared by all users of the program: tests that touch it interfere with each other and depend on execution order, instances cannot be substituted with fakes, and parallel tests race on the same instance.
quiz.explanation: Testability needs seams where fakes can be injected; a Singleton removes the seam because everyone shares the one instance and its state leaks between tests.

quiz.prompt: What does this C++ program print to stdout?
quiz.explanation: report takes a FeeModel reference but the object is a PerShareFee, so the virtual call dispatches to the override: 0.02 x 100 = 2.0, printed as 2. That dynamic dispatch is the machinery Strategy is built on.

quiz.prompt: Which API change makes this function hardest to misuse? `void process(bool buy, double qty, double px)`
options: Add a doc comment explaining that qty is in shares
Replace the bool with `enum class Side { Buy, Sell }` and wrap the parameters in a validated Fill struct
Overload it with a version taking ints
quiz.explanation: Making invalid states unrepresentable beats documenting them: with Side there is no 'true means sell?' ambiguity, and a validated Fill struct centralises the positivity check instead of hoping every caller remembers it.

flashcards.back: Define an interface for an operation, keep interchangeable implementations behind it, and let a context object hold one - swaps algorithms without touching callers (fee models, execution algos).
Modules should be open for extension and closed for modification: new behaviour arrives as new code (a new subclass), not as edits inside existing switch/if-else chains.
Domain types instead of strings/bools, units in names and types, explicit error paths, minimal public surface, names from the domain.
Adapter translates ONE foreign interface to the one your code expects; Facade simplifies a whole subsystem behind one easy front door.
